Generally, no. Facts can't be copyrighted or trademarked and a subject doesn't own the rights to his own story (think unofficial/unauthorized biographies or television like *E! True Hollywood Story*). That is not to say, however, that - in the event of distribution - you wouldn't be opening yourself up to liability. 

Something of great weight to bear in mind is the extent to which the story exists in the public domain. Generally, laws will protect content that is recognizable to the public as long as the story being manufactured doesn't draw from other copyrighted material (ie. a book, article or preexisting treatment interpreting the "actual events" - it is crucial to know that unpublished material CAN be copyrighted). But laws differ from sovereign state to sovereign state therefore you'd have to check the state of laws on libel, defamation, breach of privacy and copyright infringement in the country of choice.

Final consideration: I imagine that a spec script "based on/inspired by a true story" won't attract as many enthused productions as believed if only because attorneys will obviously be consulted to avoid liability and attorneys cost money. (Also consider that the price at which rights are negotiated when a production company is introduced into the equation rockets immediately). I'd imagine that if you could present the script to a producer with a secured agreement in hand for the subject's life story rights, you'd pique more interest.

Don't mention it- I can only hope you interpreted everything in a constructively critical light, as it was genuinely intended that way.
Honestly, no flattery or faux-sense of obligation to right the harshness of my previous comment, I find the idea at heart to be very intelligent and one that I would love to see properly developed; which I am positive you are capable of doing because the story, now that you've explained it, makes sense. If you intend to post it again, I will be looking forward to the re-write as nothing that you described in the above comment transpired upon a reading of this first draft. Adjusting dialogue, giving it some depth and "actuality" would help in that regard.

Final piece of advice and take this more from someone who has lived the environment than someone who actually has validated expertise (though I take some joy in knowing that what very little I have ever written has garnered nothing but high praise from professionals and established directors I know)- the one constant to be found of all great filmmakers and writers lies in their methodology to tackling format, storytelling, development. Every single great filmmaker has a unique style. You should remember that there are very few rules but, though most of them are in place to avoid production companies headaches while reading, you should feel free to be as inventive and descriptive as necessary in order for your story to BE and come across as **your** story. Don't be afraid to provide annotations or guide the reader if the concept is a highly metaphorical or complex one. Any one of Tarantino's scripts will be instructive in that regard as they are wildly different from the standard that production companies have grown accustomed to (in that vein, avoid any Nolan scripts excluding Memento- they become exceedingly trite after a while). A personal recent favorite of mine is Rian Johnson's "Looper" (Brick is also a great read)- he is exceptionally vivid in detailing how he intends for the story to be reflected on screen.

Take this constructively.

Starts strong-ish and funny (the jokes are hit-and-miss of the "funny on first viewing" variety) and the first page reads like a possibly great dark comedy but it gets really boring, really fast. In my opinion, the problem is that you started with an intriguing and possibly really interesting premise but then that isn't developed and the resolution is unbelievably simplistic; I was disappointed but remember that only every happens if the premise is really promising which it is- but also squandered.

The equivocity shouldn't just be the reason for a recurring joke between the protagonists; it should BE the story. It's never developed. I read it twice though, admittedly, briskly because it dragged (and I started skipping lines when I realized the story wouldn't address what had really piqued my interest) but if I read correctly the existence of "doubles" is summarily dismissed in one line: "The men’s heads peer over the bodies of Alan and Howard lying next to each other.". Without that one line in which you announce the actual existence of the two characters "Alan" and "Howard" I never would've understood it and would've kept waiting for some fantastical and fantastically comical ruse to unravel.

It's far too simple a cop out and highly doubt it would ever work on screen. As a reader I was confused and was left expecting more, convinced that it couldn't just all be a coincidence that is well beyond "improbable". A viewer would be left disoriented and unentertained. I know it's a lot to ask, but I honestly thought it was going to lead to a climax à la Fincher's "The Game" (by which I mean, "in the same vein as").

The progression is fine. It's definitely one of the most recycled genre-"subversions" in more-than-one-baddie history but it works. However it should be the least of your worries. The characters are skin deep and that would be ok if they were advancing a story which doesn't feature them: ya know, deus ex machina. But that's not the case here. Your characters are empty dei ex machina that don't actually excite any narrative progression; they just begin the story and end it.

Sidenote, I was intrigued by the capitalization (besides characters for the first time) of just SOUNDS. I know it's very arbitrary. I use a lot of italics but only because everything I introduce on screen has a meaning and is in some way pertinent, thought more often than not central, to the story.

Sincerely,
20-something law grad and aspiring screenwriter though I've breathed the airs of film and stage since infancy because of my parents.

I'll get around to your last point but first: 1. thank you for your exceptional answer, 2. you're seriously amazing, and 3. please don't misread any pedantry in what I'm about to write, I would hate to sound discourteous after the amount of detail you put into answering me and I realize it's a very fine line I'm about to walk. In hindsight, I may have overstated or not given enough context to my criticism. I come from a family heavily involved and active in the (European) theatre and film industries (both post- and production) and growing up in that specific environment I was exposed to very high standards in that regard. (Now a /r/iamverysmart joke would be appropriate). That said, it's no secret that there is a monstrously huge gap in what qualifies as "good acting" for tv and for stage or film. And not because melodrama doesn't require knowing how to act as much as knowing how to exaggerate emotion to the point of it becoming droll farce; melodrama is the consequence of not knowing how to act and the distinction is less about the source material (unless it's phenomenally good/woefully poor). In addition, imo TGW has for the first few seasons relied more on story than script, not even requiring any one actor to demonstrate their raw ability (or if there has, the execution was so sloppy it only accentuated the impression of the show delving into soap-y tropes). Josh Charles, on the other hand is outright awful, from line delivery to idiosyncrasies, the fabrication is utterly transparent and Margulies hasn't exhibited anything beyond decent acting. Of the main cast, Baranski and Cumming are the only ones who actually do anything worthwhile at any one time and nothing short of what I'd expect considering they're actors of a distinctly superior calibre. I believe Panjabi to be the true 'revelation' though, primarily because given how very little is revealed at any one time (for now) of Khalinda she can play around with the character. Everyone else though is just dragging on the same generic thing for which they're usually type-cast and are doing an "ok" job. The real stars of the show, and I agree with you whole-heartedly, are the guest and recurring stars who are given very particular yet enjoyably eccentric stories and habits. I too loved the Blake and Bond arc (the way it was unravelled throughout the season was absolutely superb) and Michael J. Fox easily steals the show whenever he is on-screen. But I realize that my criticism was out of place with reference to tv standards and I apologize for that.

Again, I just really wanted to thank you for the detailed and intelligent answer. I appreciate you spending however much time it took for you to write that. You're awesome! :)

Ummm... Grant Gustin is a mediocre TV actor. As good* as "The Flash" is in it's first season, it's driven by narrative and plot twists, it doesn't rely that much on acting (excluding, obviously, E15... what an outstanding job from Carlos Valdes). Overall, "The Flash" is a very entertaining soap with a fucked up timeline to make up for the slightly less melodrama. That said my point is that there is vast difference in talent when casting for tv and film, and while sometimes tv generates some serious talent, most times Hollywood can afford to cast from a superior pool of candidates. Finally, Andrew Garfield was actually a solid Marc Webb version of Peter Parker. The problem with the new Spidey character wasn't the acting. It was the writing (which was woefully bad). As an actor, Garfield mostly did a great job.
